title: Lesson 7: How to Study the Bible
description: You have the map and you know the story. Now it is time to learn the skill. This lesson teaches the OIA method, Observe, Interpret, Apply, and then puts you to work with your Bible open to Psalm 23.

blocks.text: In Lesson 5 you got the map of the Bible's library. In Lesson 6 you took the road trip through its one story, with Jesus at the center. This lesson hands you the skill to dig into any passage on your own.

Back in the Starting course, you learned the Three Discovery Questions: What does this passage tell me about God? What does it tell me about people? What is it calling me to do or believe? Keep using them every day. Today you will add a deeper tool to go with them.

blocks.alt: Philip running alongside the Ethiopian's chariot to explain the Scriptures

blocks.title: Philip and the Ethiopian
blocks.text:
In Acts 8, an Ethiopian official was riding home from Jerusalem. He was an important man, a court treasurer, and he had traveled a long way to worship God. Now on the dusty road home he had the scroll of Isaiah unrolled in front of him, reading aloud, hungry for truth but unable to make sense of what he saw. God sent Philip running to the side of the chariot with one simple question:

"So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, 'Do you understand what you are reading?' And he said, 'How can I, unless someone guides me?'" (Acts 8:30-31)

Philip climbed in, sat beside him, and helped him see what was already on the page. He did not add to Scripture. He showed the man how to read it. The passage was about a lamb led to the slaughter, and "beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus" (Acts 8:35).

That is what Bible study is. It is not reading faster or reading more. It is learning to see what is there, understand what it means, and let it shape how you live.

Notice who started that conversation. God sent Philip running to a man who wanted to understand. God is not hiding His Word from you, and Bible study is not a test you pass to earn His approval. It is how you hear the voice of the One who already came looking for you. And if you belong to Jesus, the Holy Spirit who inspired Scripture lives in you to help you understand it (1 Corinthians 2:12).
Three Steps: Observe, Interpret, Apply

Faithful Bible students have used this method for generations. It is called OIA, and it is three questions asked in order. What does the text say? What did it mean? How should it shape my life? The order matters. Most people jump straight to application, but the richest application comes after the honest work of observing and interpreting.
Walk through the three steps below on a psalm you may already know by heart.
Observe: What Does It Say?

Read the passage more than once. Who is speaking? What is happening? What words repeat? What surprises you? Do not interpret yet. Just notice. The last two lessons help here: know what kind of book you are reading, and where the passage sits in the Bible's story.
Interpret: What Did It Mean?

A passage cannot mean today what it never meant to its first readers. So ask what the author was saying to them, and how the passage fits its chapter, its book, and the story that leads to Jesus. Let the Bible interpret the Bible. Often the clearest explanation of a passage is somewhere else in Scripture.
Apply: How Should It Shape My Life?

Now ask how this truth reshapes the way you live. Start with what to believe before what to do. Is there a promise to trust, a sin to confess, a command to obey, or an example to follow? Obedience is your response to God's grace, never your way of earning it.
Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.

Notice the word "worker." Good Bible study takes effort, but it is the effort of a child who wants to know a Father, not a hired hand working for a wage. When you rightly handle the Word of truth, the Bible stops being a confusing book you feel guilty about and becomes a living conversation with the God who loves you.
7.1 - Which of the three steps do you tend to skip?
Practice: Psalm 23
Now it is your turn. Here is the whole psalm. Slow down and walk through it with OIA.

blocks.alt: A sheep in a field looking toward the camera, with the rest of the flock behind it

blocks.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
Observe

David wrote this psalm around 1000 BC. Before he was king, he was a shepherd who led his sheep to food and water and fought off a lion and a bear to protect them (1 Samuel 17:34-35). He knew what sheep need, and how helpless they are on their own.
7.2 - Read Psalm 23 again slowly. What do you notice that the walkthrough above did not point out?
Interpret
Let the Bible interpret the Bible. Centuries after David, Jesus picked up the same picture and said it was about Him:
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

David's shepherd risked his life for the sheep. Jesus went further and gave His life for them. Remember the Ethiopian, reading about a lamb led to the slaughter? Philip told him that Lamb was Jesus. The Good Shepherd became the Lamb, for you.
7.3 - How does John 10:11 deepen what David meant by "The LORD is my shepherd"?
Apply
7.4 - What fear do you need to lay down because the Shepherd is with you?

You just studied the Bible. You observed what was on the page, interpreted what it meant, and applied it to your life. That is not something only pastors and scholars can do. It is a skill you now have for any passage, any day, for the rest of your life.
A Skill Worth Sharing

Everything in these three lessons is transferable: the map, the road trip, and the skill. Remember the Ethiopian? He needed a Philip, someone willing to sit beside him and say, "Let me show you what I have learned about reading this book." Someday soon, someone in your life will need that from you. And when that day comes, you will be ready.
This Week's Practice

Pick a short passage this week and walk through it with OIA on your own. A few verses are enough. Try Luke 15:1-7, where Jesus tells of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find one lost sheep, or choose your own. Open your Bible, slow down, and see what God shows you.
7.5 - Write down which passage you will study with OIA this week, and when.
Lesson 7 Review

You now have the map, the road trip, and the skill. Like the Ethiopian, you do not read alone. God sends guides, gives His Spirit, and points every page to Jesus. Bible study is learning to see what is there, understand what it means, and let it shape how you live.

You also have two tools that work together. The Three Discovery Questions from the Starting course are your daily bread, simple enough to use every time you read. OIA is your weekly feast, for when you want to slow down and dig into a passage with care. Use both, and the Word of God will come alive in your hands.
In the next lesson, you will see how God's grace and mercy come to you at the cross and then flow through you to others.
Closing Reflections
What is one key thing you learned from this lesson?
What is one step you are going to take this week?
What is a prayer request for this week?
This lesson draws on the inductive study method taught in Living by the Book by Howard G. Hendricks and William D. Hendricks.
